title: Pula With a Dog 2027: Beaches, Rules, Costs & Verdict
metaDescription: Pula with a dog in 2027: dog beaches, restaurants, old town, ferries, hotel pet fees, summer heat, vet basics and EU pet passport rules for driving in.
content:
## Dog Beaches in Pula

Pula has more dog-designated shoreline than most Croatian cities. The beaches below are free to enter. Croatian beaches are public, and a "plaža za pse" is simply a stretch where dogs are explicitly allowed to swim.

### Dog's Beach Portić
Portić is the most popular dedicated dog beach in the Pula area. It lies just outside the village of Peroj on the southwestern coast. It has a white gravel shore, a dog shower, three shaded dog "shells" and free parking. All breeds and sizes are welcome. The beach is near a main road, so dogs that do not recall reliably should stay on the lead. Portić is usually quieter than the Fažana beach in summer.

### Dog Beach Verudela
This is the closest dog beach to the centre, in the Verudela resort area at Verudela 6b, about 10 minutes by car. It is a small rocky cove with dog showers, waste bins and clear signage. Sea urchins and rocky entry mean water shoes for the dog are worth considering. Cafés and the Verudela promenade are close by.

### Dog Beach Fažana
Fažana is a pebble-and-rock beach under pine trees on the village promenade. Entry is shallow and dogs are unrestricted. Waste-bag dispensers are provided, but there is no dog shower. It can be reached by car, on foot or by local bus.

### Bi Dog Beach Valbandon
About 10 km from Pula, this is a simple rocky and pebbly beach with little shade. Bring your own umbrella. Parking nearby is paid, and one of the showers is reported as unreliable.

### Other options
Valovine and Hidrobaza (Štinjan) are mentioned for pine shade and pet areas. The Kamenjak cape south of Pula has pet-friendly coves. Confirm local signage on arrival, because pet zones are rearranged between seasons.

## Are Dogs Allowed on Other Beaches in Pula?

Not everywhere. Dogs are normally barred from children's beaches, organised family beaches and Blue Flag beaches with strict rules. Look for the crossed-out dog sign. Outside swimming season, many municipalities relax enforcement, but the sign still decides.

## Old Town, Arena and Restaurants

Leashed dogs can walk through the old town. The Roman Arena and the Citadel are both reported as dog-friendly. For green space, Šijana Forest has trails and a dog park, and Monte Zaro and Mars Field (Marsovo polje) are suitable for quiet walks. Croatia's official rule for travelling dogs is a lead and a muzzle carried along. Muzzles are rarely enforced on streets, but carry one for ferries and buses.

On restaurant terraces, dogs are generally tolerated, and many cafés near the beaches welcome them. Indoor dining is at the owner's discretion, and food shops and markets do not admit dogs. Ask before sitting down.

**Summer opinion:** walking a dog on the old town's polished limestone at midday in July is a bad idea. The stone holds heat, and paws burn. Walk before 9:00 or after 19:00.

## National Parks and Brijuni

In Croatian national parks, dogs are generally allowed only on a leash and usually may not swim in protected lakes or rivers. Brijuni, the national park off Fažana, is the exception to check first. Sources conflict: some say leashed dogs are allowed, while others say dogs may not disembark. Dogs are not allowed on the tourist train or in museums and shops. Contact the park before buying tickets, or plan the Brijuni trip without the dog.

## Ferries and Catamarans

On conventional car ferries, dogs travel free on the open deck, on a lead and muzzled. Catamarans and fast ferries are stricter. Only dogs up to 8 kg in an approved bag (maximum 45 × 35 × 25 cm) are reported to be accepted. Larger dogs cannot board these services. Jadrolinija is the main operator, and some international lines need a pet ticket or cabin. Check the operator's page for the specific sailing.

## Accommodation: What Dogs Cost

Pet fees are charged per night or per stay, and are rarely included in the rate. Campsite mobile homes list the pet fee as an extra per day. Typical Istrian charges are about €5–15 per night in apartments and hotels, with a cleaning fee on some villas. Hotels may restrict dogs to certain room types, and five-star properties such as Hotel Monte Mulini in Rovinj charge a supplement. Ground-floor apartments with a yard, and private villas with fenced gardens, work best. Always confirm the pet policy in writing before paying a deposit.

## Summer Heat and Best Months

July and August regularly bring 30 °C or more, and the hottest hours are 11:00–17:00. Asphalt and stone are hotter still. Never leave a dog in a parked car. Early May to mid-June and September to early October are the best months: the sea is warm, the beaches are quieter and the heat is manageable. Winter is mild, and dogs are widely tolerated on beaches off-season.

## Vet Basics

Pula has vet clinics, and Croatian vets can issue or update an EU pet passport. Save a clinic's number and an out-of-hours option before arrival. Common problems are tick bites in woodland, sea urchin spines, and overheating. Check coats after forest walks and carry fresh water, since drinking sea water causes stomach upset. Dogs must be registered and microchipped by Croatian law, and rabies vaccination is mandatory.

## EU Pet Passport and Driving-In Rules

Croatia applies EU pet rules. Dogs arriving from EU countries need:

- An ISO 11784/11785 microchip, implanted before or on the same day as the first rabies vaccination
- A valid rabies vaccination, given at 12 weeks old or older, with a 21-day wait after the first dose before travel
- An EU pet passport issued by a licensed vet

Tapeworm treatment is not required for Croatia. Croatian authorities say a dog should be on a lead and carry a muzzle. If you drive from Italy via Slovenia, there is no pet check at Schengen borders, but carry the passport anyway. The Slovenian-Croatian border has checks at times. Non-EU arrivals, including from Great Britain, need an Animal Health Certificate, and certain countries need a titre test. A rabies vaccine dated before the microchip is treated as invalid, which is the most common error at the border. Sort the paperwork at least a month before departure.

## Verdict: How Dog-Friendly Is Pula?

Pula is very dog-friendly by Croatian standards. Four official dog beaches are within about 10 km, and the Arena, Citadel and forest parks welcome leashed dogs. Terraces are mostly tolerant, and pet-friendly rentals are plentiful. The weak points are July–August heat, rocky entries, the 8 kg catamaran limit, and uncertainty about Brijuni. Rating: 8 out of 10, best from May to June and in September.

faq.question: Is Pula dog-friendly?
faq.answer: Yes. Pula has several free dog beaches, including Portić, Verudela, Fažana and Valbandon, and leashed dogs are accepted in the old town and on many terraces. Summer heat and rocky shorelines are the main drawbacks.

faq.question: Which is the best dog beach in Pula?
faq.answer: Dog's Beach Portić near Peroj is the most popular. It has a dog shower, shaded huts, free parking and no breed or size limits. Fažana has the best pine shade.

faq.question: What documents does a dog need to enter Croatia by car?
faq.answer: An ISO microchip, a valid rabies vaccination (at least 21 days after the first dose) and an EU pet passport. Tapeworm treatment is not required.

faq.question: Can dogs go on ferries and catamarans in Croatia?
faq.answer: Dogs travel free on open decks of car ferries, on a lead and muzzled. Catamarans and fast ferries reportedly accept only dogs up to 8 kg in an approved bag.

faq.question: How much do hotels and apartments charge for a dog in Pula?
faq.answer: Typical pet fees in Istria are about €5–15 per night, sometimes with a cleaning fee. Campsites charge a separate daily pet fee, so confirm the policy before booking.

faq.question: When is the best time to visit Pula with a dog?
faq.answer: May to June and September to early October. July and August often exceed 30 °C, and stone and asphalt become too hot for paws.

quickAnswer: Pula is dog-friendly. It has several official dog beaches (Portić, Verudela, Fažana, Valbandon), leashed dogs are accepted in the old town and on café terraces, and pet fees are modest. Entry needs an ISO microchip, a valid rabies vaccination and an EU pet passport. Visit in May–June or September, because July–August heat is hard on dogs.
